title: Kids Are Stupid
author: Patrick Dempsey
summary: Dempsey extends his blue collar and white collar metaphor for education, in which the white collar worker showers before work to signal readiness and the blue collar worker showers afterward as evidence of work actually done. He uses the spaghetti and marshmallow tower exercise as the empirical hinge, contrasting the ten and a half inch towers built by MBA students against the twenty six inch towers built by kindergarteners who have no formal schooling at all. His explanation is that the children are not handicapped by the belief that understanding must precede attempt, so they simply build and observe what happens. From there he turns the word uneducated into a lever, pointing out that a chemistry student is by definition less educated in week one than in week fifteen, and that the conventional sequencing argument would forbid application until understanding arrives. He notes the same logic being applied to student use of AI while rarely being applied to textbooks or teachers. The essay ends on higher education's response to AI, which he reads as doubling down on critical thinking and the humanities, a move that smuggles the foundational knowledge requirement back in and keeps the sector stuck at the morning shower.
points: The shower metaphor does real analytical work here, separating credentials that signal preparation from evidence that work has actually been performed.
Dempsey uses the marshmallow tower research as a concrete counterexample to the claim that more schooling yields better performance on an open ended build task.
His central reversal is that one is never too uneducated to learn by doing, but can become too educated to believe that doing is a legitimate way to learn.
He catches an inconsistency in AI policy debates, since the demand that students understand before using AI is not applied to textbooks, worksheets or teachers.

He reads higher education's pivot to human skills and critical thinking as a restatement of the same prerequisite logic, because critical thinking is then said to require foundational knowledge first.
quotes: White-collar workers shower before work. Blue-collar workers shower after work.

This has been done hundreds of times, and the research has found that MBA students—which we do want to clarify have some 18-plus years of formal education—will build, on average, 10.5-inch-tall towers.

They don't "know enough" to understand that the "correct" process is to create a plan, and determine roles, and allocate resources—to really build a foundation, a theory if you will, of how best to construct the tallest tower possible.
No, these imbecilic kids just start building! They don't know what the tape is for. They aren't trying to figure out a theory of string and tension and distribution.
As an aside, I see this idea quite a bit in discussions about AI use specifically. Students shouldn't use AI until they have a sufficient understanding of the concepts.
you are never too uneducated to do stuff to learn, but it does appear possible to be too educated to think you can just do stuff and learn.
And guess what critical thinking requires? You guessed it: foundational knowledge! You can't think critically without understanding what you're thinking about!
It seems higher ed just cannot move past the morning shower. It is obsessed with the appearance of preparedness over the actual evidence of practice.
